questions.q: Blue can make at most 40 coats or 160 shirts. How many shirts does Blue give up to make 1 coat?
questions.fb: Divide what is given up (shirts) by what is gained (coats): 160 ÷ 40 = 4. Revisit Step 2 of the worked example in the Learn tab.

questions.q: Red can make at most 120 coats or 240 shirts. How many coats does Red give up to make 1 shirt? (give a decimal)
questions.fb: The opportunity cost of a shirt is the inverse of the coat calculation: coats given up ÷ shirts gained = 120 ÷ 240 = 0.5. Check Step 2 again.

questions.q: Using the figures above, which country has the comparative advantage in coats?
questions.ok: Correct: Red gives up 2 shirts per coat, Blue gives up 4, so Red's opportunity cost is lower.
questions.fb: Compare opportunity costs, not total output. Red gives up 2 shirts per coat and Blue gives up 4, so Red is the lower-cost producer of coats. Re-read the table in Step 2.

questions.q: Complete the definition: a country has a comparative advantage in a good when it can produce it at a lower ________ than another country.
questions.fb: The definition is about opportunity cost, not about producing more. A country has a comparative advantage when it gives up fewer other goods to make the good. See the Tips & keywords tab.

questions.q: A country can make every good using fewer resources than its trading partner. Could it still gain from trade?
opts: Yes, because it is likely to have a lower opportunity cost in some goods
No, because it has nothing to gain from a weaker country
Only if the other country has an absolute advantage in something
Only if it imports every good
questions.ok: Correct: the gain comes from comparative, not absolute, advantage.
questions.fb: Absolute advantage in everything does not stop trade being worthwhile. Gains come from specialising where the opportunity cost is lower. See 'A country can have an absolute advantage in everything and still gain from trade' in the Learn tab.
questions.model: Yes, because it is likely to have a lower opportunity cost in some goods

questions.q: In the worked example a coat costs Red 2 shirts and Blue 4 shirts to make. Between which rates of exchange could both countries gain?
questions.ok: Correct: Red wants more than 2 shirts per coat, Blue will pay less than 4.
questions.fb: Each side must receive a better deal than making the good itself. Red will not sell a coat for under 2 shirts, and Blue will not pay more than 4. Revisit Step 5.

questions.q: Red makes only coats (120) and Blue makes only shirts (160). How many shirts does the world produce?
questions.ok: Correct: only Blue makes shirts, so the world total is 160.
questions.fb: After specialising, only Blue makes shirts, so world shirt output is Blue's maximum of 160. See Step 4.

questions.q: At an exchange rate of 3 shirts per coat, Red sells 40 coats. How many shirts does Red receive?
questions.fb: Shirts received = coats sold × shirts per coat = 40 × 3 = 120. See Step 6.

questions.q: Which of these is a limitation of a country specialising heavily according to comparative advantage?
opts: It could become over-dependent on a few exports
Consumers have less choice and higher prices
questions.ok: Correct: over-dependence leaves the country exposed to price falls and shocks.
questions.fb: Heavy specialisation can leave a country over-dependent on a few exports, so a fall in world prices or demand may hurt it badly. The other options describe the opposite of the theory's benefits. See the Exam questions tab.
questions.model: It could become over-dependent on a few exports

questions.q: What name is given to the rate at which one country's goods exchange for another's?
questions.fb: The term is 'terms of trade'. Add it to your keyword list in the Tips & keywords tab.
